title: Question 3: Governmental Entity Discrimination and Preferential Treatment Prohibited

context.text: Placed on the ballot by the legislature as Assembly Joint Resolution 102 (second consideration; it first passed in the 2023-24 session). The 2026 votes were Assembly 54-45 on January 13, 2026 and Senate 18-15 on January 21, 2026. The governor has no veto over constitutional amendments.

question.text: Question 3: “Governmental entity discrimination prohibited. Shall section 27 of article I of the constitution be created to prohibit governmental entities in the state from discriminating against, or granting preferential treatment to, any individual or group on the basis of race, sex, color, ethnicity, or national origin in public employment, public education, public contracting, or public administration?”

summary.text: The amendment would create Article I, Section 27, defining “governmental entity” broadly (state, municipalities, the UW System, technical colleges, public school districts, and other state and local bodies) and providing that such an entity “may not discriminate against, or grant preferential treatment to, any individual or group on the basis of race, sex, color, ethnicity, or national origin in public employment, public education, public contracting, or public administration.” Per Ballotpedia's reproduction of the text, it exempts action required to keep eligibility for federal programs and bona fide sex-based qualifications reasonably necessary to normal operations, and includes a severability clause. No fiscal estimate was found.

measure.yesMeans: Creates Section 27 of Article I prohibiting governmental entities in Wisconsin from discriminating against, or granting preferential treatment to, any individual or group on the basis of race, sex, color, ethnicity, or national origin in public employment, public education, public contracting, or public administration.
measure.noMeans: Does not add Section 27 to the constitution; existing federal and state anti-discrimination laws and programs are unchanged.

argumentsFor.text: State Sen. Steve Nass: "Preferential treatment to any individual or group is wrong, no matter who it targets or what the reason. Past discrimination, however wrong, cannot be corrected with more discrimination. Old wounds cannot be healed by inflicting new ones."

Dan Lennington, Vice President and Deputy Counsel, Wisconsin Institute for Law & Liberty, in Assembly Judiciary Committee testimony: "The United States Constitution and the Wisconsin Constitution are built on a foundation of racial equality. No one may be granted a preference or denied a benefit based on race."

State Rep. Dave Murphy (R-Hortonville), co-author, in committee testimony: "This isn't new policy—it's a return to Wisconsin's core values. Our state constitution should affirm what we all believe: everyone deserves a fair shot."

argumentsAgainst.text: State Sen. Dora Drake (D-Milwaukee): "It limits our own ability to help you — the public — and will make things worse." State Sen. Chris Larson (D-Milwaukee) said the amendment "will make addressing disparities significantly harder to achieve."

Amanda Merkwae, policy and advocacy director, ACLU of Wisconsin: "What the amendment is ultimately designed to do is eliminate proactive programs geared towards equity, like minority and women-owned business recruitment, or targeted workforce development, or retention initiatives in higher education that are designed to ensure that everyone gets a fair shot."
Debra Cronmiller, executive director of the League of Women Voters of Wisconsin: "This amendment is not prohibiting governmental entity discrimination."

currentLaw.text: The Wisconsin Constitution has no section like the proposed Article I, Section 27. The UW Law School's State Democracy Research Initiative explains that if the amendment fails, state and federal equal protection principles would continue to prohibit many forms of discrimination and classification-based preferential treatment, and that the amendment's effect on specific programs would likely be resolved in future litigation.

supporters.text: Wisconsin Institute for Law & Liberty (WILL; Vice President Dan Lennington testified in support of AJR 102 on November 5, 2025)
State Sen. Steve Nass and Rep. Dave Murphy (R-Hortonville), the resolution's authors, who testified for it

researchNotes: Wisconsin publishes no state voter pamphlet with pro/con arguments, and the Wisconsin Elections Commission pages returned HTTP 403 to automated requests and were not bypassed, so the question text is taken from the enrolled joint resolution on docs.legis.wisconsin.gov, which states the ballot question verbatim (machine-checked; each enrolled resolution labels its question 'Question 1' because each was enacted separately). Official vote tallies are from the Legislature's bill history page. Arguments are floor remarks and a legislator's press release. The Wisconsin Institute for Law & Liberty's supporting statement (WILL page returned 403) and the opposing coalition letters were not fetched at the time of the first pass; testimony and statements fetched later are now used as additional arguments. The amendment's subsections (federal-program exemption, bona fide sex-based qualifications, severability) are from the enrolled resolution. WPR's voter guide confirms there are exactly three statewide questions on the Nov. 3, 2026 ballot and their numbering. Added October 19, 2026: no official fiscal estimate and no registered-committee campaign-finance totals were found (the Wisconsin Ethics Commission's campaign-finance system could not be queried; the Wisconsin Justice Initiative says WILL is the only organization registered in support), so those fields are omitted. WILL's own website returned HTTP 403 and was not bypassed; its stance is shown by its Legislature testimony. Current law is summarized from the UW Law School explainer, not from an official analysis, because the Legislative Reference Bureau analysis describes only the proposal. The League of Women Voters filing is a draft-style document with margin comments; only its stated position is used.
